notes: Liberal Party in ruling slot 2 (Lleras Restrepo) using the MD Liberal sprite; Conservatives in partner slot 1 as the National Front co-governing party. ANAPO in slot 20 (MD populist slot). FARC follows MD in slot 4 (PCC of Gilberto Vieira described as its parent); ELN slot 5, Maoist EPL slot 19. MRL dissolved in 1967 and is omitted; ANUC in slot 18.

0.name: Departamento Administrativo de Seguridad
0.text:
The Administrative Department of Security was created in 1960 to replace the discredited political police of the dictatorship and has become the National Front's main intelligence service. On 1 January 1970 it watches the guerrillas, the communist unions, the student movement and the growing following of Rojas Pinilla under the state of siege.

Trained and advised by the United States, the DAS thinks in terms of counter-insurgency and the doctrine of national security. Its chiefs favour emergency decrees, military justice for civilians and quiet cooperation with American agencies. Its leverage lies in its files, its informants and the near-permanent state of siege.

1.name: Partido Conservador Colombiano
1.text:
The Colombian Conservative Party, founded in 1849, shares power with the Liberals under the National Front pact of 1958, which alternates the presidency and divides offices equally. The next president must be a Conservative, and the official candidate for April 1970 is Misael Pastrana Borrero, backed by former president Mariano Ospina Pérez against dissidents Belisario Betancur and Evaristo Sourdís.

The party defends the Catholic Church, property, order, regional notables and close alignment with the United States. It is split between Ospinistas and the harder Laureanista wing of Álvaro Gómez Hurtado. Its leverage lies in rural clientele networks, the clergy and its guaranteed half of the state.

2.name: Partido Liberal Colombiano
2.text:
The Colombian Liberal Party, founded in 1848, holds the presidency through Carlos Lleras Restrepo, elected in 1966 as the third president of the National Front. Lleras governs as a reforming technocrat, having pushed through the constitutional reform of 1968, and Alfonso López Michelsen, whose dissident movement rejoined the party in 1967, serves as his foreign minister.

The Liberals stand for planned development, agrarian reform through INCORA, peasant organisation, a stronger executive and a secular, modernising state firmly tied to the Alliance for Progress. They distrust both Rojas Pinilla's populism and the guerrillas. Their leverage lies in the presidency, the cities and the trade unions.

3.name: Confederación de Trabajadores de Colombia
3.text:
The Confederation of Workers of Colombia was founded in the 1930s under the Liberal 'Revolution on the March' of Alfonso López Pumarejo and remains the trade-union arm of liberal reformism. Purged of its communist unions in 1960, it is led in 1970 by José Raquel Mercado and affiliated to the American-backed inter-American labour organisation ORIT.

The CTC stands for collective bargaining, social security, labour law reform and an alliance with the Liberal Party against both the oligarchy and the communists. It is pro-Western and anti-communist. Its leverage lies in the unions of the ports, transport and public services and its voice in Liberal councils.

4.name: Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia
4.text:
The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia grew out of the communist peasant self-defence zones such as Marquetalia, bombarded by the army in 1964, and took their present name in 1966. Commanded by Manuel Marulanda Vélez with the party ideologue Jacobo Arenas, they field a few hundred fighters in the mountains of Tolima, Huila and Cauca in 1970.

The FARC are the armed wing of the pro-Soviet Colombian Communist Party of Gilberto Vieira, which pursues the 'combination of all forms of struggle'. They demand agrarian reform, an end to the National Front and alignment with the Soviet camp. Their leverage lies in remote peasant colonisation zones far from the state.

5.name: Ejército de Liberación Nacional
5.text:
The National Liberation Army was founded in July 1964 in the hills of Santander by students trained in Cuba under Fabio Vásquez Castaño. It gained fame when the revolutionary priest Camilo Torres joined and died in combat in 1966, and in 1970 it remains a small, harshly disciplined foco in the Magdalena Medio and San Vicente de Chucurí.

The ELN follows the Cuban road of armed struggle, mixes Guevarism with Christian radicalism, and wants to overthrow the National Front, nationalise oil and land and break with the United States. Its leverage lies among radical students, the oil workers of Barrancabermeja and rebellious clergy.

6.name: Los Hispanistas
6.text:
Los Hispanistas are the Catholic-traditionalist intellectuals, clergy and Conservative notables who cling to the integralist ideals of the Laureano Gómez era. Clustered in Bogotá's Catholic colleges, the Instituto Caro y Cuervo and the provincial Conservative press, they see 1970 as a year of moral decay.

They reject both Soviet communism and American liberalism, Protestant missions and consumer culture, and look instead to Hispanic Catholic civilisation and Franco's Spain. They want a confessional corporate state, Church control of education and censorship of modern culture. Their leverage lies in the pulpits, the universities and the old Conservative families.

7.name: Los Peruanistas
7.text:
Los Peruanistas are a current of colonels and majors who watch with admiration the Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces in Peru, which seized power in 1968 and nationalised American oil. They see their symbol in General Alberto Ruiz Novoa, the reformist war minister dismissed in 1965 for criticising the oligarchy.

They believe the National Front is too corrupt and too tied to Washington to defeat the guerrillas, and want the army to impose agrarian reform, nationalise oil and mines and rule above the parties. Their leverage lies in the officer schools and the frustration of an army bogged down in counter-insurgency.

8.name: Comunidad Chií de Maicao
8.text:
The Shia Community of Maicao is formed by Lebanese traders from the south of Lebanon who have settled in the border town of La Guajira, trading with Venezuela. In 1970 they remain a few hundred families, praying in homes and shops and keeping Ashura in private.

They look to the Lebanese Shia awakening led by Imam Musa al-Sadr, combining religious revival with demands for dignity and social justice. In Colombia they seek tolerance, community schools and good relations with local authorities. Their leverage lies in commercial wealth and in remittances that tie Maicao to the villages of south Lebanon.

9.name: Los Fieles de Karbala
9.text:
Los Fieles de Karbala are a small circle of devout young Lebanese Shia in Maicao and Barranquilla who reject the easy assimilation of their elders. In 1970 they import religious books from Najaf and Beirut, insist on strict mourning rites and send sons abroad to study under Shia clerics.

They believe that society must be ruled by religious law and by learned clergy, and see Western culture and the Christian majority around them as threats to the faith. They have no political ambitions in Colombia itself but follow the struggles of the Middle East closely. Their leverage lies in piety and kinship.

10.name: Los Notables de Maicao
10.text:
Los Notables de Maicao are the Sunni merchant elders, Palestinian, Syrian and Lebanese, who dominate the wholesale trade of the Guajira border town and its contraband routes to Venezuela. In 1970 they finance prayer rooms and Quranic lessons for their children and maintain discreet ties with the consuls of the Arab monarchies.

They stand for orthodox, quietist Islam, obedience to established authority and good relations with Colombian officials and the party bosses of the Guajira. They avoid politics and admire Saudi Arabia as guardian of the holy places. Their leverage lies in money, credit and their indispensable place in the border economy.

11.name: Círculo de la Umma
11.text:
The Círculo de la Umma is a tiny group of young Arab-Colombian students and shop assistants in Maicao and Bogotá, radicalised by the Arab defeat of 1967 and the rise of the Palestinian fedayeen. In 1970 they read Sayyid Qutb in smuggled Arabic pamphlets and meet in back rooms.

They believe the Muslim world must reunite under a restored caliphate and that both Western capitalism and atheist communism are enemies of the faith. In Colombia they seek converts and funds for Palestine rather than power. Their leverage is negligible, limited to a few families and their links to the Middle East.

12.name: Juventud Musulmana del Caribe
12.english: Muslim Youth of the Caribbean Coast
12.text:
Juventud Musulmana del Caribe brings together educated sons and daughters of Arab merchant families in Barranquilla, Maicao and Cartagena who studied in Beirut, Damascus or Cairo and returned with the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood. In 1970 they organise study circles, Arabic classes and charity drives.

They present Islam as a complete and modern way of life, calling for moral reform, religious education and a recognised Muslim association in Colombia, while respecting the constitution. They support Palestine and distrust both superpowers. Their leverage lies in education, family wealth and their bridge between the Arab community and Colombian society.

13.name: Departamento Nacional de Planeación
13.text:
The National Planning Department, reorganised by Carlos Lleras Restrepo in 1968, is the brain of the National Front's development state. Its economists, many trained in the United States and advised by the World Bank and the Alliance for Progress, draft investment plans, control public spending and design the agrarian and fiscal reforms of 1970.

The planners believe in rational, technocratic government above the quarrels of party bosses and the noise of Congress, and they welcome the stronger executive created by the 1968 reform. They are pragmatic toward East and West. Their leverage lies in their control of the budget and their access to the presidency.

14.name: Conferencia Episcopal de Colombia
14.text:
The Episcopal Conference of Colombia unites the bishops of one of the most Catholic countries in the world, where the Concordat of 1887 still gives the Church a privileged role in education, marriage and the mission territories. The Medellín conference of Latin American bishops in 1968 has unsettled it, and in 1970 the hierarchy faces the rebel priests of the Golconda group.

The bishops defend Catholic education, the family, the Concordat and social peace, and condemn both communism and violent revolution while cautiously preaching social reform. Their leverage lies in the parishes, the schools, the Catholic union federation UTC and the respect of the Conservative party.

15.name: Federación Nacional de Cafeteros de Colombia
15.english: National Federation of Coffee Growers of Colombia
15.native_full: Federación Nacional de Cafeteros de Colombia
15.text:
The National Federation of Coffee Growers of Colombia, founded in 1927, is a state within the state: it manages the National Coffee Fund, buys and exports the harvest that earns most of the country's foreign exchange and builds roads, schools and banks in the coffee zones. Its manager Arturo Gómez Jaramillo is one of the most powerful men in Colombia in 1970.

The Federation is ruled by the great growers and exporters of Antioquia, Caldas and the Valle, who want price stability, the International Coffee Agreement, low taxes and no radical land reform. It is firmly pro-Western. Its leverage lies in money, credit and the coffee economy itself.
15.wiki: National Federation of Coffee Growers of Colombia

16.name: Asociación Nacional de Industriales
16.text:
The National Association of Industrialists was founded in Medellín in 1944 by the textile, beverage and steel magnates of Antioquia and has become the voice of Colombian private industry. In 1970 it bargains with the government over tariffs, exchange rates and the Andean Pact signed in 1969.

ANDI favours private enterprise, open markets, fiscal restraint and foreign investment, and resists price controls, state enterprises and union militancy. It is staunchly anticommunist and closely tied to American capital. Its leverage lies in the factories of Medellín, Bogotá and Cali and in its influence on both traditional parties.

17.name: Instituto de Desarrollo de los Recursos Naturales Renovables
17.english: Institute for the Development of Renewable Natural Resources
17.native_full: Instituto de Desarrollo de los Recursos Naturales Renovables
17.text:
The Institute for the Development of Renewable Natural Resources was established in 1968 to manage Colombia's forests, fisheries, wildlife and national parks. In 1970 its young biologists and foresters are mapping the destruction of the Andean forests, the Magdalena basin and the Caribbean mangroves, and pressing for new protected areas in the Amazon and on the Pacific coast.

The institute's staff and their allies in the universities call for national parks, reforestation, controls on logging and hunting, and protection of indigenous lands. They are technocrats rather than militants. Their leverage lies in scientific expertise, international conservation support and the president's faith in planning.

18.name: Asociación Nacional de Usuarios Campesinos
18.text:
The National Association of Peasant Users was launched by decree of Carlos Lleras Restrepo in 1967 to enrol peasants as users of state agrarian services and to build mass support for land reform. By 1970 hundreds of thousands of smallholders, tenants and landless labourers are registered in municipal committees, and the movement prepares its first national congress.

ANUC demands land redistribution, credit, cooperatives and an end to the power of the great estates. Created by the state, it is already slipping out of government control as radical leaders push for land occupations. It stands outside both blocs. Its leverage lies in sheer numbers across the countryside.

19.name: Ejército Popular de Liberación
19.text:
The Popular Liberation Army is the armed wing of the Communist Party of Colombia (Marxist-Leninist), the pro-Chinese party that split from the pro-Soviet communists in 1965. Launched in 1967 in the Alto Sinú and Alto San Jorge regions of Córdoba, it lost its founder Pedro Vásquez Rendón in 1968 and has suffered heavy losses by 1970.

The EPL follows Mao's doctrine of protracted people's war, encircling the cities from the countryside, and denounces both American imperialism and Soviet revisionism. It wants agrarian revolution and a people's democratic republic. Its leverage lies among the peasants and colonists of Córdoba and Urabá.

20.name: Alianza Nacional Popular
20.text:
The National Popular Alliance was founded in 1961 by General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, the dictator overthrown in 1957, to fight the National Front from within its rules by running candidates under Liberal and Conservative labels. His political rights restored in 1967, Rojas is the Conservative-labelled challenger in the April 1970 election, with his daughter María Eugenia Rojas as chief organiser.

ANAPO mixes Catholic nationalism, social welfare, price controls and fierce attacks on the oligarchy, promising the poor cheap food and housing. It draws on the urban poor, small traders and former soldiers. Its leverage lies in a mass movement of the barrios that is growing alarmingly fast.

21.name: Los Pájaros
21.text:
Los Pájaros take their name from the Conservative hired killers who terrorised Liberal peasants in the Valle del Cauca during La Violencia. In 1970 the label covers the surviving gunmen, local bosses and ultraconservative landowners who preserve the networks of the 1950s and resent the bipartisan peace.

They believe Liberals, communists and Protestants are enemies of God and nation, and want an authoritarian Catholic state without parties, enforced by armed militias. They despise the National Front as a betrayal. Their leverage lies in fear, rural impunity and the willingness of some landowners to pay for private violence.

22.name: Fuerzas Militares de Colombia
22.text:
The Military Forces of Colombia, comprising the army, navy and air force, returned power to civilians in 1958 after the junta that replaced Rojas Pinilla, and have since accepted civilian supremacy under the National Front. In 1970 they are absorbed in counter-insurgency against the FARC, ELN and EPL under a near-permanent state of siege.

Shaped by American training programmes and the Plan Lazo of the early 1960s, the officer corps holds to the doctrine of national security, combining civic action with repression. It is fiercely anticommunist and pro-Western. Its leverage lies in its role in internal order, military courts for civilians and its say in defence policy.

23.name: Los Realistas de Pasto
23.text:
Los Realistas de Pasto are a circle of Catholic traditionalists, antiquarians and old families in the southern city of Pasto, which fought for the Spanish Crown against Bolívar and still honours the royalist guerrilla leader Agustín Agualongo. In 1970 they gather in cultural societies and confraternities, keeping alive the memory of the viceroyalty.

They regard the republic as a Masonic and liberal mistake and dream of a Catholic monarchy under the Spanish Bourbons, whose heir Prince Juan Carlos was named Franco's successor in 1969. They are politically insignificant but socially respectable. Their leverage lies in regional pride, Church ties and Hispanist cultural networks.
